method: Each law sets the left and right channel gains from the pan position: t = (pan + 100) / 200 runs from 0 at hard left through 0.5 at the centre to 1 at hard right, and the pan angle is a = t x 90 degrees. The -3 dB constant-power law uses gL = cos(a) and gR = sin(a), so gL^2 + gR^2 = 1 at every position and a centred signal sits 3.01 dB down in each channel. The -6 dB linear law uses gL = 1 - t and gR = t, so gL + gR = 1 and a centred signal sits 6.02 dB down in each channel. The -4.5 dB compromise is the geometric mean of the two, gL = sqrt((1 - t) cos(a)) and gR = sqrt(t sin(a)), which leaves each channel about 4.5 dB down at the centre. Gains are relative to the unpanned signal, reported in dB and as a percentage of amplitude, with the left-minus-right difference. The mono fold-down adds the two channels as amplitudes, 20 log10(gL + gR), the result for identical in-phase content summed to one channel. The two-speaker level adds their powers, 10 log10(gL^2 + gR^2), assuming the speakers radiate independently at the listening position. Constant power therefore holds the two-speaker level flat but folds up to 3.01 dB hot in mono, the linear law holds the mono sum flat but loses up to 3.01 dB on two speakers, and the compromise splits both errors at about 1.51 dB. Consoles and DAWs vary in detail, some compensating the taper and some not. The page models the gain taper only: it does not measure loudness and assumes one mono source panned between two channels. Pan positions must be plain decimals, optionally with a leading decimal point and a minus sign; values outside -100 to 100 percent and unknown laws are refused with the reason. Results carry two decimals. Everything is calculated in the browser; nothing is uploaded, stored or sent anywhere.
